# Public Datasets

## ResStock 2025 Release 1 New

The updated dataset builds on the End Use Savings Shapes methodology, with 28 packages. New major updates include the additions of Hawaii and Alaska, electric vehicles, updated utility rates, HVAC demand flexibility, electric panel estimations, and improved geothermal heat pump modeling. For details about the ResStock model used to create this dataset, see the Technical Reference Guide and the short readme paper which has a description of all packages, important assumptions, and changes from the last dataset release. A summary of how column names have changed in this dataset since 2024 Release 2 is also available. The geothermal heat pump results from this AMY 2018 2025 Release 1 dataset are shown in the Evaluating Geothermal Performance for the U.S. Building Stock Tableau dashboard with ComStock geothermal heat pump results.

For more information on this dataset, and other ResStock datasets, see our User Resource Website which has examples, FAQs, measure documentation and more. Have additional questions or comments? Email our team at ResStock@nlr.gov.

### ResStock 2025 Release 1

The measure packages included in this release include:

  1. Natural Gas Furnace 95% AFUE
  2. Propane Furnace 95% AFUE and Fuel Oil Furnace 88% AFUE
  3. Reference Space Heating and Air Conditioning Upgrade Circa 2025
  4. Cold Climate Air-Source Heat Pump
  5. Dual Fuel Heat Pump

  7. Residential Two-Stage Geothermal Heat Pump (4.0 COP, 20.5 EER)
  8. Residential Variable-Speed Geothermal Heat Pump (4.4 COP, 30.9 EER)
  9. Heat Pump Water Heater
  10. Natural Gas Water Heater
  11. Advanced Air Sealing
  12. Attic Floor Insulation
  13. Duct Sealing and Insulation

## Summer Peak Increase from Cold CLimate Heat Pump in ResStock 2025 Release 1

“Summer peak savings” came into question when looking closely at the ResStock 2025 Release 1 results for upgrade 4, the cold climate air source heat pump (ccASHP) upgrade. To start, there are two different definitions of “summer peak savings”

  1. Sector peak - this is the peak electricity demand over a timestep for the residential sector in a particular geographical region (e.g., state, county, national, etc.). It is the sum of the timeseries energy consumption for all building models in the sector on a timestep-basis.
  2. Individual model peak - this is the peak electricity demand over a timestep for a specific building model in the ResStock dataset. Here are some of the ResStock team’s notes about summer peak savings:
     * Peak savings is the difference between the baseline peak of the specific season and the upgrade’s peak of the specific season.
     * The baseline and upgrade scenario peaks do not necessarily occur on the same calendar day, hour, and timestep.
The ccASHPs are sized to the maximum of the heating and cooling loads. In many cases, this can result in more cooling capacity than baseline AC systems. Therefore, they can maintain setpoint better than the existing AC systems.

In ResStock, HVAC systems that are not heat pumps have the heating and cooling components each independently sized to the respective heating or cooling load according to design conditions. Heat pumps are one physical piece of equipment that perform both heating and cooling. They can either be sized using ACCA Manual S or to the maximum load of the heating and cooling loads. The ccASHP upgrade is sized to the maximum of the heating and cooling load according to the HVAC design conditions of the geographic location it is located. In cold climates, the heating load often drives the heat pump capacity so many ccASHPs in the dataset end up with a much larger cooling capacity than the baseline AC system.

Models that the ccASHP applied to and are 100% conditioned in the baseline sample have an average increase in delivered cooling energy of ~2200 kBtu/yr (5%) compared to baseline and an average increase in the rated cooling capacity of ~2.5 tons (85%).

content.text:

## Summer Peak Increase from Cold CLimate Heat Pump in ResStock 2025 Release 1

“Summer peak savings” came into question when looking closely at the ResStock 2025 Release 1 results for upgrade 4, the cold climate air source heat pump (ccASHP) upgrade. To start, there are two different definitions of “summer peak savings”

  1. Sector peak - this is the peak electricity demand over a timestep for the residential sector in a particular geographical region (e.g., state, county, national, etc.). It is the sum of the timeseries energy consumption for all building models in the sector on a timestep-basis.
  2. Individual model peak - this is the peak electricity demand over a timestep for a specific building model in the ResStock dataset. Here are some of the ResStock team’s notes about summer peak savings:
     * Peak savings is the difference between the baseline peak of the specific season and the upgrade’s peak of the specific season.
     * The baseline and upgrade scenario peaks do not necessarily occur on the same calendar day, hour, and timestep.
The ccASHPs are sized to the maximum of the heating and cooling loads. In many cases, this can result in more cooling capacity than baseline AC systems. Therefore, they can maintain setpoint better than the existing AC systems.

In ResStock, HVAC systems that are not heat pumps have the heating and cooling components each independently sized to the respective heating or cooling load according to design conditions. Heat pumps are one physical piece of equipment that perform both heating and cooling. They can either be sized using ACCA Manual S or to the maximum load of the heating and cooling loads. The ccASHP upgrade is sized to the maximum of the heating and cooling load according to the HVAC design conditions of the geographic location it is located. In cold climates, the heating load often drives the heat pump capacity so many ccASHPs in the dataset end up with a much larger cooling capacity than the baseline AC system.

Models that the ccASHP applied to and are 100% conditioned in the baseline sample have an average increase in delivered cooling energy of ~2200 kBtu/yr (5%) compared to baseline and an average increase in the rated cooling capacity of ~2.5 tons (85%).

L67@P5: Executive Summary
L68@P5: The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact,
L69@P5: market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. “Measures” refers to energy efficiency retrofits
L70@P5: that can be applied to buildings during modeling.
L71@P5: An “end-use savings shape” is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building
L72@P5: and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It
L73@P5: results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas,
L74@P5: propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.
L75@P5: ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data
L76@P5: sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the
L77@P5: annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States.
L78@P5: The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018.
L79@P5: Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is
L80@P5: available in (Reyna, et al. 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are
L81@P5: available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles
L82@P5: (https://www.nlr.gov/buildings/end-use-load-profiles.html) project.
L83@P5: This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure—cold climate heat pump
L84@P5: upgrade.
L85@P5: The cold climate heat pump upgrade demonstrated 30% total site energy savings (3,535 TBtu)
L86@P5: for the U.S. residential building stock (Figure 7). These savings are primarily attributed to:
L87@P5: • 53.7% stock total heating savings (3,173.8 TBtu)
L88@P5: • 10.1% stock total cooling savings (132.7 TBtu).

L67@P5: Executive Summary
L68@P5: The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover a majority of the high-impact,
L69@P5: market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. “Measures” refers to energy efficiency retrofits
L70@P5: that can be applied to buildings during modeling.
L71@P5: An “end-use savings shape” is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building
L72@P5: and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It
L73@P5: results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas,
L74@P5: propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.
L75@P5: ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data
L76@P5: sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the
L77@P5: annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States.
L78@P5: The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018.
L79@P5: Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is
L80@P5: available in (Reyna, et al. 2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are
L81@P5: available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles
L82@P5: (https://www.nlr.gov/buildings/end-use-load-profiles.html) project.
L83@P5: This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure—cold climate heat pump
L84@P5: upgrade.
L85@P5: The cold climate heat pump upgrade demonstrated 30% total site energy savings (3,535 TBtu)
L86@P5: for the U.S. residential building stock (Figure 7). These savings are primarily attributed to:
L87@P5: • 53.7% stock total heating savings (3,173.8 TBtu)
L88@P5: • 10.1% stock total cooling savings (132.7 TBtu).

L176@P8: This upgrade measure replaces any existing non-shared ducted heating and air
L177@P8: conditioning system with a variable-speed ducted air-source heat pump (ASHP)
L178@P8: with electric resistance backup. If the unit does not have air conditioning, the unit

L180@P8: measure upgrade package is denoted in the ResStock options_lookup.tsv as the
